Some people may lose consciousness or stiffen and convulse, while others remain awake but experience changes in movement, awareness, sensation or behaviour. Rescue medicines, often benzodiazepines, may be prescribed to stop prolonged seizures or clusters. Anti‑epileptic Medicines

Epilepsy is a neurological condition characterised by recurrent seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. It is common but often misunderstood, and people with epilepsy can live full lives with appropriate support.
Risk factors for epilepsy include age, family history, head injury, vascular disease, dementia, brain infection and febrile seizures in childhood. In many cases the cause is unknown, but when a cause is identified it may relate to genetics, brain injury, structural abnormalities, infections, prenatal injury or developmental disorders.
Common triggers for seizures include hormonal changes, trauma, fever, alcohol and other substances, psychological stress, sleep deprivation and flashing lights. Each person has their own set of triggers, and understanding these helps to reduce seizure risk.
Seizures can be classified as generalised, focal or provoked. Generalised seizures affect both hemispheres of the brain and include tonic–clonic, absence, myoclonic, tonic and atonic types. Focal seizures begin in a specific brain region and may spread to become generalised. Provoked seizures result from an acute insult such as head injury or metabolic disturbance.
During a seizure, the priority is to keep the person safe using the principles STAY – SAFE – SIDE – DON’T – CONSIDER – CALL. Most seizures stop on their own, but prolonged seizures require emergency rescue medication and in some cases hospital treatment and intensive care.
Treatment aims to prevent or reduce seizures. Anti‑epileptic drugs are the mainstay of therapy, but surgery, nerve stimulators and the ketogenic diet are options for some individuals. Lifestyle management – including avoiding triggers, getting enough sleep, reducing alcohol, managing stress and adhering to medication – plays a key role in seizure control.
Prolonged seizures can cause complications such as cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, brain injury and injury from falls or aspiration. Awareness and prompt action help reduce these risks.

Urinary incontinence is the unintentional loss of urine. It is a symptom, not a disease, and can have different causes and patterns. Recognising the type of incontinence helps inform the appropriate management plan.
Stress Incontinence
Stress incontinence occurs when physical activities such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting or exercising increase pressure in the abdomen and cause urine to leak through a weak sphincter or pelvic floor. It is common after childbirth, pelvic surgery or during menopause.
Urge Incontinence
Urge incontinence is characterised by a sudden, strong urge to urinate followed by involuntary bladder contractions and urine leakage. It is often associated with overactive bladder syndrome and may be triggered by running water, cold temperatures or suddenly standing up.
Overflow Incontinence
Overflow incontinence happens when the bladder does not empty completely, leading to frequent dribbling or a constant trickle of urine. It may result from an obstruction (such as enlarged prostate), weak bladder muscles or nerve damage.
Functional Incontinence
Functional incontinence occurs when physical or cognitive impairments prevent a person from reaching the toilet in time, even though bladder function may be normal. Examples include severe arthritis, poor mobility, or confusion from dementia.
Total Incontinence
Total incontinence describes continuous and complete loss of bladder control. Causes can include congenital abnormalities, spinal cord injury or fistulas between the urinary tract and other organs. Management often involves catheterisation.
Anyone experiencing urinary incontinence should be offered assessment and support.
